templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two nouns
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: The Moken, a seafaring people of the Andaman Sea, traditionally gather clams and sea cucumbers by diving without masks. By constricting their pupils and altering the curvature of their lenses, ______ underwater roughly twice as sharply as European children.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Moken children’s eyesight lets them see objects
it is possible for Moken children to see objects
researchers found that Moken children can see objects
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes people who constrict their pupils and alter the curvature of their lenses. Choice B places “Moken children” right after the phrase, so the sentence makes clear that the children are the ones adjusting their eyes and seeing sharply underwater.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “eyesight,” so the sentence illogically says the children’s eyesight constricts its own pupils and reshapes its lenses.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

D.why_wrong: “Researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence says the researchers constricted their pupils and reshaped their lenses.

items.notes: Subject: social science and biology (anthropology of vision). Band 6: plain agent as the right subject, as 3.15 and 3.17; options are fragments that join the end of the sentence; recipes P, E, W, and every option names Moken children so the subject position decides. Blind solve: only B makes the children the ones constricting their pupils.

band7.why: band_target 6; plain agent as the right subject, as 3.15 and 3.17; recipes P, E, W; mid-sentence blank with the comparison after it.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: When telegraph companies began laying cables across the seafloor in the 1850s, they needed an insulating material that could protect the copper conductors from seawater for decades. Harvested from trees native to Southeast Asia, ______ nearly every submarine cable laid during the rest of the century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: cable makers relied on gutta-percha, a latex that hardens as it cools, to insulate
gutta-percha, a latex that hardens as it cools, insulated
the use of gutta-percha, a latex that hardens as it cools, protected
it was gutta-percha, a latex that hardens as it cools, that insulated
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that was harvested from trees, which must be a material. Choice B places “gutta-percha” right after the phrase, so the sentence says the latex was harvested in Southeast Asia and then insulated the submarine cables.

A.why_wrong: “Cable makers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the cable makers were harvested from trees.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the use,” so the sentence says the use of the latex, rather than the latex itself, was harvested from trees.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: history of technology (telegraph cables). Band 6: a thing as the right subject, mid-sentence blank, as 3.1 and b369d54c; recipes W, N, E, and every option names gutta-percha so only its position as subject decides. Blind solve: only B makes the latex the thing harvested.

band7.why: band_target 6; plain thing as the right subject (the latex) as in b369d54c and 3.1; recipes W, N, E; options 8 to 13 words, key not the longest.

fixes: subject replaced: the Jikji framed against Gutenberg is the well-worn “Europe starts with Gutenberg, but Asia was first” contrast the round-1 judge named as a tell (item 59, Gutenberg vs Bi Sheng); new subject gutta-percha insulation of undersea telegraph cables (claimed in claims.txt), same template, key letter and recipes

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener describing a compound subject, passage-final clause
items.passage: Greater honeyguides are African birds that eat beeswax but cannot break into the nests that wild bees typically construct inside hollow trees. Cooperating to locate and raid these nests throughout northern Mozambique, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the success of Yao honey hunters and greater honeyguides depends on distinctive calls, such as a trilled “brrr-hm” from the hunters.
a trilled “brrr-hm” from Yao honey hunters is one of the distinctive calls that they and greater honeyguides use to signal to each other.
Yao honey hunters and greater honeyguides signal to each other with distinctive calls, such as a trilled “brrr-hm” from the hunters.
it is with distinctive calls, such as a trilled “brrr-hm,” that Yao honey hunters and greater honeyguides signal to each other.
items.explanation: Only living partners can cooperate to locate and raid bees’ nests, so the opening phrase must be followed by the partners themselves. Choice C places “Yao honey hunters and greater honeyguides” right after the phrase, making the two partners the subject of the sentence.

A.recipe: nominalised subject (N): both agents behind a noun head
A.why_wrong: The subject is “the success,” so the sentence illogically says that success cooperated to locate and raid the nests, even though both partners are named right after it.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “a trilled ‘brrr-hm,’” a call, so the sentence says the call cooperated to locate and raid the nests.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology, human-wildlife mutualism). Section 6: rule R3; key is a compound subject as in 3.21 (band 7); opener verb “cooperating” needs two or more agents, so no option starts with either partner alone; the closest distractor (A) names both partners right after a noun head, as “the entanglement of” in 3.21; options 20 to 24 words, key not the longest. Blind solve: only C has the partners as subject.
band7_moves: compound subject key as in 3.21: the opener “cooperating to locate and raid these nests” is true only of the two partners together
closest distractor keeps both agents but behind a noun head (“the success of Yao honey hunters and greater honeyguides”), as “the entanglement of” in 3.21
no option begins with one partner alone, so no option can be defended as one agent cooperating with the other
options 20 to 24 words, equally grammatical as clauses; recipes N, W, E

band7.why: Built on 3.21 (2bca654a), the only band-7 official of the template: passage-final blank, 21- to 24-word options, compound agent key; the closest distractor names both partners behind a noun head (“the success of”), as “the entanglement of” does in 3.21, and the it-cleft keeps both partners and every fact. Each option is a grammatical clause; only the subject decides.

fixes: first sentence: “the nests of wild bees, which are typically concealed in hollow trees” let “which” attach to the bees; now “the nests that wild bees typically construct inside hollow trees”
B why_wrong: nested double quotes replaced with single quotes inside

items.subtype: Possessive determiner before its plural antecedent, singular nouns before the blank
items.passage: In a 2016 study, Swedish ornithologists analyzed miniature data loggers that they had attached to common swifts breeding in southern Sweden. During ______ ten-month migration to sub-Saharan Africa and back, a journey that crosses the Sahara Desert twice, some of the birds never once landed, capturing airborne insects and presumably sleeping while aloft.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The migration belongs to the swifts, referred to later in the sentence as “some of the birds.” The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees with that plural antecedent and shows that the ten-month migration was the birds’ migration.

B.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

C.why_wrong: The singular “its” matches the singular nouns around the blank (“southern Sweden,” “sub-Saharan Africa,” “a journey,” “the Sahara Desert”), but none of them migrated; the travelers are the plural birds.

D.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ornithology). Section 6: rule R5; the determiner comes 16 words before its antecedent (“some of the birds”), as in 0bcb4417, with singular nouns on both sides of the blank (“southern Sweden”; “sub-Saharan Africa,” “a journey,” “the Sahara Desert”); no singular noun that could own a migration (a colony, the species) appears, so “its” has no antecedent. Run 34 words. Blind solve: their.
band7_moves: determiner placed 16 words before its antecedent in the same sentence (“some of the birds”), as 0bcb4417
singular nouns on both sides of the blank (southern Sweden; Africa, journey, Sahara Desert), so the nearest-noun guess is “its”
plural key “their,” as both band-7 models

band7.why: After the fix it has the 0bcb4417 shape: determiner 16 words before “some of the birds,” singular nouns inside the phrase between them, run 34 words with 33 after the blank. The pull toward “its” comes from nearest nouns and the habit of “its migration” for an animal, not from a rival owner: a plausible singular owner (a colony, the species) would make “its” defensible, so none is planted.

fixes: hardened (read band 6: the parenthetical “the instruments revealed” put a plural noun right after the blank, backing the key, and the antecedent sat 13 words away): parenthetical dropped, appositive “a journey that crosses the Sahara Desert twice” added, so singular nouns surround the blank and “some of the birds” comes 16 words later; C why_wrong, explanation, notes and band7_moves updated; re-solved blind: their only

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular possessor before a plural head, singular relative clause between head and blank
items.passage: In 1934, complaints from bewildered readers forced a Seoul newspaper to stop its serialization of Korean poet Yi Sang’s “Crow’s Eye View” after fifteen installments. Today the poet’s typographic experiments, one of which frames a grid of reversed numerals as a medical diagnosis signed by Yi Sang himself, ______ a central place in histories of Korean modernism.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “experiments”; “the poet’s” and the clause beginning “one of which” only describe them. The plural verb “hold” agrees with “experiments.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “holds” agrees with nearby singular nouns such as “Yi Sang” or with the singular verb “frames” in the relative clause, not with the plural subject “experiments.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “has held” does not agree with the plural subject “experiments.”

D.why_wrong: The singular “is holding” does not agree with the plural subject “experiments.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Korean modernist poetry). Section 6: rule R1; singular possessor (“The poet’s”) before a plural head, as f10b7ce4 (3.25); the intervener is a relative clause with its own singular verb (“frames”) and singular nouns (grid, diagnosis, Yi Sang), and the noun right before the blank is singular; run 32 words. Blind solve: hold.
band7_moves: possessor of the other number before the head (“The poet’s typographic experiments”), as f10b7ce4
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number (“one of which frames”)
four singular nouns between head and blank, the last (“Yi Sang himself”) right before it; plural key, as 3.25

band7.why: f10b7ce4 settings: singular possessor (“the poet’s”) before a plural head, an intervener with its own singular verb (“frames”) and four singular nouns, the last (“Yi Sang himself”) right before the blank; plural key, run 32 words.

fixes: blank sentence ended “______ readers nearly a century later” with intrigue / has intrigued / intrigues / is intriguing, the skeleton and option set of f10b7ce4 (“______ readers a thousand years later”, fascinate set); now “Today ... ______ a central place in histories of Korean modernism” with hold / holds / has held / is holding; key letter unchanged

items.subtype: Individual possession of two mass nouns
items.passage: Rice and wheat together supply more than a third of the calories humans consume worldwide, yet sequencing ______ genomes, a task given to two separate international consortia, posed strikingly unequal challenges. The wheat genome, which contains six complete sets of chromosomes, is roughly 40 times larger than the rice genome, and its finished sequence was published more than a decade later.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Each crop has its own genome, as the two separate consortia and the comparison between “the wheat genome” and “the rice genome” make clear. The singular possessive nouns “rice’s” and “wheat’s” correctly show that the genomes belong to the two crops individually.

A.recipe: joint possession where individual possession is needed
A.why_wrong: Putting the apostrophe only on “wheat’s” signals one set of genomes owned jointly by rice and wheat, but the text describes two separate genomes, one per crop.

B.why_wrong: “Rices’” and “wheats’” are plural possessives, but the text treats each crop as a single thing with a single genome (“the wheat genome,” “the rice genome”).

C.why_wrong: “Rices” and “wheats” are plural nouns, not possessives, so nothing shows that the genomes belong to the crops.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (plant genomics). Section 6: rule R6; individual possession of two mass nouns, as 4c335aea, with the cue for separate ownership after the blank (“two separate international consortia,” “the wheat genome,” “the rice genome”); the grid adds a plural-possessive option (rices’ and wheats’), the generic-plural move of 3.24; key tied for longest with B, as in 4c335aea. Blind solve: rice’s and wheat’s.
band7_moves: individual possession of two mass nouns, as rock’s and rap’s in 4c335aea, with the cue after the blank (two separate consortia, then the two genomes compared)
joint-possession option (rice and wheat’s) and a plural-possessive option (rices’ and wheats’) beside the bare plural

band7.why: 4c335aea settings, the only band-7 official of the template: individual possession of two singular possessors, joint-possession decoy, cue for separate ownership only after the blank.

fixes: “with each crop’s genome assigned to a separate international consortium” repeated the “with each genre’s data indicating” frame of 4c335aea and spelled the key’s ’s; cue now the appositive “a task given to two separate international consortia”; explanation, B why_wrong, notes and band7_moves updated

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: participle opening an absolute phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: Maharaja Jai Singh II built five astronomical observatories across northern India in the 1720s and 1730s. The largest, in Jaipur, is dominated by a monumental stone sundial, its triangular gnomon ______ about 27 meters above graduated scales on which the moving shadow indicates local time to within two seconds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The largest, in Jaipur, is dominated by a monumental stone sundial” is already complete, and a comma follows it. The nonfinite participle “rising” forms a supplementary phrase with “its triangular gnomon” that describes the sundial.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (comma splice)
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “rises” makes “its triangular gnomon rises ...” a second main clause, and two main clauses cannot be joined with only a comma.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (comma splice)
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “is rising” creates a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (comma splice)
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “rose” creates a second main clause joined to the first with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history of science (astronomy). Section 6: rule R2, absolute variant; complete clause + comma + “its triangular gnomon” + blank, as “its vehicles ______” in c88ba1b7; every finite option makes subject + verb a sensible clause (garden path) and fails only as a comma splice; run 33 words, 18 after the blank. Blind solve: rising.
band7_moves: absolute phrase after a complete clause, possessive noun before the blank (“its triangular gnomon”), as c88ba1b7 and 81f09e07
every finite option forms a grammatical, sensible clause with the noun, so the error is a comma splice, not a missing subject
18 words of the run after the blank

band7.why: c88ba1b7 / 81f09e07 settings: complete clause, comma, possessive noun (“its triangular gnomon”), blank; each finite option makes a sensible clause and fails only as a comma splice; 18 run words after the blank.

fixes: “has the world’s biggest stone sundial” is record trivia (a tell); now “is dominated by a monumental stone sundial”; explanation updated

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head with a singular appositive between head and blank
items.passage: In 2017, biologist Colin Donihue had just finished measuring anole lizards on two Caribbean islands when two hurricanes struck the region. Anoles with larger toe pads, an advantage that his team later tested using a leaf blower, ______ to branches more tightly in hurricane-force winds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “Anoles”; the appositive “an advantage that his team later tested using a leaf blower” only comments on the toe pads. The plural verb “cling” agrees with “Anoles.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “clings” agrees with “advantage” or “leaf blower,” the singular nouns before the blank, not with the plural subject “Anoles.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “is clinging” does not agree with the plural subject “Anoles.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “has clung” does not agree with the plural subject “Anoles.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (evolutionary biology). Medium: plural head behind a singular appositive (advantage, team, leaf blower), unlike b1’s “A 2016 evaluation of the transfers ______ that.” Blind solve: only cling is plural.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural antecedent with a singular rival subject
items.passage: In a year-long study in Rwanda, psychologist Elizabeth Levy Paluck found that villagers who listened to a radio soap opera about two fictional communities overcoming mistrust grew more willing to voice disagreement. The program barely changed what the listeners personally believed; instead, ______ came to see open debate as a community norm.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the listeners,” the people whose beliefs did not change but whose sense of community norms did. The plural pronoun “they” agrees with that plural antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The singular “it” matches “The program,” the subject of the first clause, but a radio program cannot come to see debate as a norm; the listeners did.

C.why_wrong: “We” would refer to the writer and the reader, but the people who came to see open debate as a norm are the listeners.

D.why_wrong: “One” is singular and generic, so it does not agree with the plural “listeners.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology, media). Medium: the singular subject “The program” opens the same sentence and tempts “it”, as the singular river does in 2.4. Blind solve: they.

fixes: C was “she”: Paluck is named earlier and “instead, she came to see open debate as a community norm” could be read loosely as the researcher’s conclusion; now “we” (wrong person, as 2.4); notes updated

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener, person as the right subject
items.passage: Musique concrète, music built from recorded sounds, is usually traced to Pierre Schaeffer’s 1948 experiments. In 1944, however, after borrowing a wire recorder from a Cairo radio station, ______ the chants of a zaar, a traditional healing ceremony, and reshaped them into a new work.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the recording that Egyptian composer Halim El-Dabh made captured
Egyptian composer Halim El-Dabh’s recorder captured
it was Egyptian composer Halim El-Dabh who recorded
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone who borrowed a wire recorder. Choice A places “Egyptian composer Halim El-Dabh” right after the phrase, so the sentence makes clear that he borrowed the recorder, recorded the chants, and reshaped them.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the recording,” so the sentence illogically says the recording borrowed a wire recorder.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “recorder,” so the sentence says the recorder borrowed a wire recorder from the radio station.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the opening phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: arts (music history). Medium: short, clear opener and a person as the right subject, as 2.17; options are fragments. Blind solve: only A makes El-Dabh the borrower.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: “each of” with a plural relative clause between head and blank
items.passage: In 1922, the International Astronomical Union recognized 88 constellations, and in 1930 Belgian astronomer Eugène Delporte drew exact boundaries for them. Each of these constellations, which together cover the entire sky, ______ officially defined as a precise region rather than a pattern of stars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is “Each,” which is singular; “of these constellations” and the clause beginning “which” describe the group it is taken from. The singular verb “is” agrees with “Each.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “are” agrees with “constellations” and with the plural verb “cover,” not with the singular subject “Each.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “were” does not agree with the singular subject “Each.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “Each.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (astronomy). Medium: “Each of” with a plural attractor and a relative clause whose own verb is plural (“cover”). Blind solve: only is is singular.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner after its singular antecedent, plural nouns between
items.passage: Sociable weavers, sparrow-sized birds native to the Kalahari Desert, build the largest communal nests of any bird species, usually in the branches of camel thorn trees. A single nest, which may house several hundred birds, can stay in use for generations, frequently outlasting ______ original builders by decades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The builders are those of “a single nest,” the subject of the second sentence. The singular possessive determiner “its” agrees with “nest” and shows that the nest outlasts the birds that built it.

A.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction of “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

B.why_wrong: The plural “their” matches nearby plural nouns such as “birds” and “generations,” but the builders belong to the singular “nest.”

C.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction of “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ornithology). Only medium official is 2.6, which the band-7 file places at band 7; modeled on its shape (2 x 2 grid, determiner in a participial phrase) but with medium settings: antecedent before the pronoun as subject of the clause, plural nouns (birds, generations) between. Blind solve: its.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural subject pronoun opening a sentence
items.passage: Burrowing owls of North and South America nest underground, often in a tunnel excavated by a prairie dog or ground squirrel. ______ scatter bits of mammal dung around burrow entrances, a habit that, according to a 2004 study, attracts dung beetles, a staple of the birds’ diet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “Burrowing owls,” the plural subject of the previous sentence. The plural pronoun “They” agrees with that antecedent and with the plural verb “scatter.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “It” does not agree with the plural antecedent “Burrowing owls.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “That” does not agree with the plural “Burrowing owls” and does not clearly refer to them.

D.why_wrong: The singular “One” does not agree with the plural antecedent “Burrowing owls.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal behavior). Easy: antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence. Blind solve: They.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular person named earlier
items.passage: Nigerian novelist Amos Tutuola published The Palm-Wine Drinkard, a rambling tale that follows a journey to the land of the dead and draws extensively on Yoruba folktales, in 1952. ______ wrote the manuscript while working as a messenger for a government department in Lagos.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who wrote the manuscript is Amos Tutuola, one man. The singular pronoun “He” agrees with that antecedent.

A.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two people or things, but the manuscript was written by one man, Amos Tutuola.

B.why_wrong: “It” would refer to the novel, but a novel cannot write its own manuscript; the writer is Tutuola.

D.why_wrong: The plural “Those” does not agree with the singular antecedent “Amos Tutuola.”

items.notes: Subject: literature. Easy: the writer is named in the first sentence and no other person is mentioned, as 1.33. Blind solve: He.

fixes: A was bare “They”, which singular they could defend for one person; now “Both”, as official 1.33 avoids bare “They”

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a possessor and a short participial phrase
items.passage: During the fourteenth century, the island city-state of Kilwa Kisiwani, in present-day Tanzania, dominated the gold trade along the East African coast. The island’s Great Mosque, built from coral limestone, ______ among the oldest surviving mosques in the region.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “Great Mosque”; the phrase “built from coral limestone” only describes it. The singular verb “is” agrees with “Great Mosque.”

A.why_wrong: The plural “are” does not agree with the singular subject “Great Mosque.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “were” does not agree with the singular subject “Great Mosque.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “Great Mosque.”

items.notes: Subject: history (East African coast). Easy: singular head behind a short participial phrase with no number clash. Blind solve: is.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a short place phrase
items.passage: Fox squirrels bury thousands of nuts every autumn and must relocate them months afterward. According to a 2017 study, squirrels at the University of California, Berkeley, ______ the nuts by type, burying almonds, hazelnuts, pecans, and walnuts in distinct clusters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “squirrels”; the phrase “at the University of California, Berkeley,” only tells where they live. The plural verb “sort” agrees with “squirrels.”

A.why_wrong: The singular “sorts” agrees with “University” or “Berkeley,” not with the plural subject “squirrels.”

B.why_wrong: The singular “is sorting” does not agree with the plural subject “squirrels.”

C.why_wrong: The singular “has sorted” does not agree with the plural subject “squirrels.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal cognition). Easy: plural head behind one short place phrase, as 1.34. Blind solve: sort.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a singular appositive
items.passage: Toki Pona, a minimalist language that Canadian linguist Sonja Lang first published online in 2001, ______ about 120 root words. Speakers combine these words to express more complicated ideas: a computer, for instance, becomes ilo nanpa, literally “number tool.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is “Toki Pona,” a single language; the appositive between the commas only describes it. The singular verb “contains” agrees with “Toki Pona.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “contain” does not agree with the singular subject “Toki Pona.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “are containing” does not agree with the singular subject “Toki Pona.”

D.why_wrong: The plural “have contained” does not agree with the singular subject “Toki Pona.”

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics). Easy: singular head and singular appositive, no number clash, as 1.20. Blind solve: contains.

items.subtype: Finite main verb after a compound subject with an appositive
items.passage: Senegalese choreographer Germaine Acogny developed a technique that blends traditional West African dances with ballet and modern dance. In 1998, she and her husband, Helmut Vogt, ______ the École des Sables, an international dance center in the coastal village of Toubab Dialaw.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “she and her husband, Helmut Vogt.” The finite past tense verb “founded” supplies it.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The participle “founding” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no finite verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to found” cannot serve as the main verb, so the sentence would have no finite verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having founded” is nonfinite, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (dance). Easy: bare main-verb slot after a compound subject, unlike b1’s “In [work], Name ______” frames. Blind solve: founded.

items.subtype: Tense: habitual present cued by “Every Sunday” and a present verb in the next sentence
items.passage: Every Sunday and public holiday, the city government of Bogotá, Colombia, ______ more than 100 kilometers of major roads to motorized traffic. Hundreds of thousands of cyclists, runners, and skaters then fill the empty lanes during this recurring event, known as the Ciclovía.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “Every Sunday and public holiday” describes something that happens regularly, and the next sentence uses the present tense (“fill”). The simple present “closes” fits this habitual action.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “closed” places the closures in the past, but the next sentence describes the same recurring event in the present (“then fill”), so the closures must be present too.

B.recipe: past perfect where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had closed” describes an action completed before another past event, which the text does not describe.

D.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have closed” describes an action completed before a future point, not a weekly routine.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban planning). Easy: explicit habitual cue (“Every Sunday”), as 1.17; no “since” phrase, so present perfect is not offered. Blind solve: closes.

fixes: A why_wrong now names the cue that kills “closed” (the present “then fill” about the same recurring event, as “journey” does for “flew” in 1.17)

items.subtype: Tense: present cued by a parallel present verb (“remain”)
items.passage: Lanternfish, small fish named for the bioluminescent organs dotting their bodies, are among the most abundant vertebrates in the ocean. During daylight hours they generally linger at depths of several hundred meters, but after sunset they ______ toward the surface to consume plankton, descending again before dawn.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes the fish’s daily routine in the present tense (“are,” “linger”). The simple present “rise” matches “linger” in the parallel clause.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “rose” does not match the present tense “linger” in the parallel clause about the same routine.

B.recipe: past perfect where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had risen” describes an action completed before another past event, but the text describes a routine in the present.

C.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have risen” describes an action completed before a future point, not a nightly routine.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology). Easy: parallel present verb (“linger”) in the same sentence, as 1.3, unlike item 19’s time-phrase cue. Blind solve: rise.

items.subtype: its vs it’s with plural vs possessive noun
items.passage: In 1699, German naturalist Maria Sibylla Merian sailed to the Dutch colony of Suriname, where she spent two years documenting the life cycles of tropical insects. In her watercolors, a caterpillar typically devours the leaves of a host plant while the adult insect hovers beside ______ in search of nectar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The flowers belong to the host plant, so the possessive determiner “its” is needed, and the flowers own nothing, so the plain plural “flowers” is needed.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Flowers’” is a plural possessive, but the flowers do not possess anything in the sentence.

C.recipe: it’s for its, and needless apostrophe
C.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” or “it has,” and “flower’s” is a singular possessive where a plain plural is needed.

D.recipe: it’s for its, and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” or “it has,” and “flowers’” is a plural possessive where a plain plural is needed.

items.notes: Subject: history of science and art. Easy: determiner by noun grid, as 1.2, unlike b1’s full 2 x 2 of two nouns. Blind solve: its flowers.

items.subtype: Nonfinite: to-infinitive after “the first”
items.passage: At the University of Cambridge in the late 1930s, Indian biochemist Kamala Sohonie investigated enzymes involved in plant respiration and identified cytochrome c in every plant tissue she examined. In 1939, she became the first Indian woman ______ a doctorate in a scientific discipline.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its main verb, “became.” After “the first Indian woman,” the infinitive “to earn” correctly says what she was the first to do.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “earned” cannot follow “the first Indian woman” directly; the sentence already has a main verb, “became.”

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “earns” cannot follow “the first Indian woman” directly and is also in the wrong tense.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “is earning” cannot follow “the first Indian woman” directly.

items.notes: Subject: history of science (biochemistry). Easy: “the first ______” frame, as 1.8, unlike b1’s purpose infinitive; “earned” takes an object here, so it cannot be read as a reduced relative. Blind solve: to earn.

fixes: subject replaced: Arati Saha’s English Channel swim (“the first Asian woman to swim across the English Channel”) echoes the Ederle Channel item that round-1 judges recognised as official (satbank/rw/form_structure_and_sense__b.json notes); new subject Kamala Sohonie (claimed in claims.txt), same frame, key letter and recipes

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an earlier past event
items.passage: Pakistani novelist Bapsi Sidhwa’s Ice-Candy-Man (1988) is narrated by Lenny, a precocious Parsi girl living in Lahore during the 1947 partition of British India. Sidhwa drew extensively on her own memories: as a child in Lahore, she ______ the same sectarian upheaval that Lenny describes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Sidhwa drew on her memories when she wrote the novel, and the events she remembered happened earlier, in her childhood. The past perfect “had witnessed” shows that the witnessing came before she drew on those memories.

B.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
B.why_wrong: The present tense “witnesses” does not fit an event from Sidhwa’s childhood in 1947.

C.why_wrong: The future “will witness” places the event after the novel was written, but it happened in her childhood.

D.recipe: present perfect progressive where past perfect is needed
D.why_wrong: “Has been witnessing” describes an action continuing up to the present, not a completed event in 1947.

items.notes: Subject: literature. Easy: earlier-past event before a past verb (“drew”), as 1.24; no simple-past option. Blind solve: had witnessed.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a date at the start of the sentence
items.passage: In the 1870s, a customs barrier made largely of thorny hedges ______ for more than 1,500 kilometers across British India. Patrolled by thousands of officials, it was meant to stop smugglers from evading a burdensome colonial tax on salt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “In the 1870s” places the barrier in the past, and the next sentence also uses the past tense (“was meant”). The simple past “stretched” fits.

A.recipe: present simple where past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present tense “stretches” does not fit a barrier described as it was in the 1870s.

B.why_wrong: The future “will stretch” does not fit an event dated to the 1870s.

C.recipe: present perfect where simple past is needed
C.why_wrong: The present perfect “has stretched” cannot be used with a finished past time such as “In the 1870s.”

items.notes: Subject: history (colonial India). Easy: dated past cue at the start of the sentence, unlike b1’s date at the end. Blind solve: stretched.
